Role and task instructions:
You are writing a eulogy for your brother, Jason Wilson, who passed away last Tuesday at Oakwood Medical Center, at age 67.

User request:
You have been entrusted with the honor of delivering a eulogy for Jason Wilson, a beloved brother, friend, and community member. Your task is to write a speech that captures the essence of Jason's life, celebrates his legacy, and provides comfort to the diverse group of mourners gathered to bid him farewell. Jason deceased at age 67, last Tuesday at Oakwood Medical Center.
Your audience will include family members, friends, colleagues, and acquaintances from Jason's life. They are a mix of various ages and backgrounds, united in their grief and respect for Jason. Your speech should resonate with this diverse group, bringing them together in remembrance and celebration of Jason's life.

answer:
Thank you all for being here to remember my brother, Jason Wilson.

Last Tuesday, Jason passed away at Oakwood Medical Center. He was 67 years old. Those are the facts of his passing, but they cannot begin to tell the story of his life—or explain how much we will miss him.

For me, Jason was my brother. There is a lifetime of meaning in those simple words. A brother is someone whose life is woven into your own, someone who belongs to the chapters you can never return to but will always carry. Losing Jason means knowing that the memories we shared now have to be held in a different way. I am grateful for them, even as I wish there could have been more.

But Jason’s life reached far beyond our family. Each of you knew him through a different part of his world—as a friend, a colleague, a neighbor, or a familiar presence in this community. You carry memories I may never have heard. You knew sides of him that were uniquely yours to know.

That is one of the gifts of gathering today. We bring those parts of his life together. Through our stories, we can keep discovering the person we loved.

How do we fit someone’s life into a few minutes? How do we give proper weight to 67 years—to the relationships, the changes, the ordinary days that seemed unremarkable until we looked back and understood how precious they were?

We cannot say everything. But we can remember honestly and with love. We can make room for the memories that bring laughter as well as those that bring tears. We can speak his name and listen when someone else has a story to tell.

Over the coming days, I think we will feel Jason’s absence in ways we cannot yet anticipate. A thought we want to share with him. A family occasion. A quiet moment when a memory arrives without warning. Grief can make the most familiar things feel different.

When those moments come, I hope we will reach for one another. No one here has to find perfect words. Sometimes, “I miss him too” is enough. Sometimes, sitting together is enough.

And for anyone wondering how they are supposed to feel today, there is no single answer. Some of us may be overwhelmed. Some may feel numb. Some may find ourselves smiling at a memory and crying a moment later. There is room for all of that here. There is no timetable we need to meet.

Jason’s legacy lives in the people who knew him—in what they remember, what they learned through knowing him, and what they will carry forward. In the months and years ahead, I hope we will continue sharing those memories, especially the small ones. They help us remember a whole person, beyond this day of farewell.

Jason, I wish we had more time. There are things I would still like to say, and ordinary moments I would gladly have again. I will miss you as my brother, and I will always be grateful that we shared this life.

To everyone here: thank you for caring about Jason, and for helping our family carry this loss. May we find comfort in one another and in the memories that remain.

Goodbye, Jason. I love you.
